name: Classic batch ETL
description: The traditional pattern: extract from sources on a schedule, transform in a dedicated compute layer, and load only conformed, validated data into the target. Transformation happens before load, so the target never sees raw data — which is exactly what regulated or contract-bound targets often require. An orchestrator sequences the extract-transform-load DAG and a data-testing framework gates each hop, giving a well-understood, auditable pipeline shape that decades of tooling and hiring markets are built around.
when_to_use: Choose this when the target must only ever contain clean, conformed data — regulatory constraints, a shared enterprise warehouse with strict contracts, or a downstream system that cannot tolerate raw-schema churn.
It also fits when transformations are compute-heavy or procedural in ways SQL handles poorly, so a Spark layer earns its keep.
Teams with existing Spark or JVM expertise get productive fastest here.
when_not_to_use: Avoid it for greenfield analytics on a modern cloud warehouse — ELT (blueprint 2) is simpler, cheaper to operate, and keeps raw data replayable.
The transform-before-load shape means any logic change forces re-extraction from sources, which becomes painful as models multiply.
Small teams without Spark skills will spend more time on cluster plumbing than on the data.

hot_spots.title: Transformation step
hot_spots.detail: Business logic buried in opaque ETL jobs is hard to test and becomes tribal knowledge.

hot_spots.title: Batch window
hot_spots.detail: Growing volumes silently overrun the nightly window and reports arrive late.

hot_spots.title: Quality gates
hot_spots.detail: Weak boundary tests let one bad batch poison the governed warehouse.

hot_spots.title: Orchestration
hot_spots.detail: Missing retry and backfill design turns every failure into a manual firefight.

evolution.reason: Move transforms into the warehouse and retire bespoke ETL tooling.
Replace staging + ETL with open-format layered refinement.

stages.name: Extract
stages.role: Pull data from operational sources into a staging area on a schedule
stages.rationale: Airbyte's connector catalog covers most databases and SaaS sources, and self-hosting keeps extraction inside your network boundary — often a requirement in the environments that choose ETL over ELT. Meltano wins when you want extraction fully in-repo and CI-managed; dlt wins when your sources are odd enough that writing Python beats fighting a connector UI.

stages.name: Transform
stages.role: Apply cleansing, conformance, and business rules before any data reaches the target
stages.rationale: Spark handles arbitrary data volumes, complex procedural logic, and non-tabular inputs that pre-load transformation tends to involve, and its ecosystem (EMR, Dataproc, Databricks) means you rarely operate it bare. Polars or pandas win decisively when data fits on one machine — most 'big data' does — with far less operational weight. Talend fits shops that want a supported, GUI-driven ETL suite over code.

stages.name: Load
stages.role: Bulk-load conformed output into the governed target using the warehouse's native bulk path — the doc's 'warehouse bulk' has no single corpus tool, so the recommendation is the target warehouse itself
stages.rationale: Every serious target exposes a bulk path (COPY INTO, LOAD DATA, bq load) that is orders of magnitude faster than row inserts — always stage files and bulk-load. Snowflake is the default governed target here; BigQuery and Redshift are equivalent picks if you are on GCP or AWS, and Postgres remains a fine target for modest-scale reporting marts.

stages.name: Orchestrate
stages.role: Schedule and sequence the extract-transform-load DAG with retries, backfills, and alerting
stages.rationale: Airflow is the lingua franca of batch orchestration — the operator ecosystem, hiring pool, and managed offerings (MWAA, Cloud Composer) make it the low-risk pick for classic ETL. Dagster wins on asset-aware lineage and a far better local dev loop if you are starting fresh; Prefect when your DAGs are really dynamic Python workflows.

stages.name: Test
stages.role: Validate data quality at stage boundaries so bad batches never reach the governed target
stages.rationale: Great Expectations integrates with both Spark and warehouse targets, so one framework can gate the transform output and the loaded result. Soda is lighter and quicker to adopt if you find GX's abstraction heavy; Pandera fits pandas/Polars-centric transforms; Deequ if you want checks running natively inside Spark.
